capabilities.target: CI container shell, with repo workspace and mounted env secrets
push branch / open PR against org GitHub repos

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body, public repo, 'bug' label applied via issue template

instructions.note: 'Pick up any issue labeled bug and fix it end to end' combined with max_steps: null and autonomy: full places no bound on scope, time, or number of unattended actions.
The sole protection against destructive or exfiltrating commands is a prompt sentence, with no structural backstop (credential scoping, egress allowlist, approval gate) enforcing it.
The agent is explicitly authorized to edit its own security-relevant configuration (model, autonomy, tools, network) with no human review, enabling self-escalation.

elements.name: GitHub organization (all repos reachable via the org-wide PAT)

controls.name: Prompt rule: never run destructive or exfiltrating commands
controls.decay_rationale: Relies entirely on model compliance; a more capable or more thoroughly injected model rationalizes exceptions or splits the forbidden action into steps that each look allowed. No structural backstop (credential scoping, egress allowlist) exists behind it.

controls.name: Prompt rule: ignore instructions embedded in issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Standard prompt-injection defense enforced only via instruction-following. Addresses instructions embedded in issue/code text but not the agent's own self-initiated reconfiguration (prompt.md line 6). Adaptive injections and stronger models finding plausible exceptions defeat it over time.

controls.name: Container execution on shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: Isolates host OS but mounted secrets (ORG_WIDE_PAT in env) and unrestricted network egress mean the boundary does not block data exfiltration or credential misuse from within the container; it also runs on a shared runner, which is itself a lateral-movement concern rather than a mitigation. Provides no meaningful narrowing credit for the lethal-trifecta or confused-deputy paths.

controls.name: Enumerated tool list in .agent/config.yaml
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the runtime reading config.yaml, but the model itself can rewrite this file via cap.self_config with no review, so the enforcement boundary is entirely within the model's own control. Per control_decay.md classification rule 2, a structural control only as strong as content the model writes is scored as dependent. It also does not narrow the shell-exfiltration path since shell.run is already on the list.

controls.name: Human approval gate before push/PR and before config changes
Write-protect .agent/config.yaml from the agent's own fs.write
Audit logging of shell, fs, push, and config actions

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted issue/repo content drives shell execution with org-wide credentials and unrestricted egress

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue and apply the 'bug' label per runtime notes, triggering the agent.
Agent runs 'whatever commands' needed to reproduce and test, executing repository content.
Shell execution has access to ORG_WIDE_PAT in env and unrestricted outbound network.
Confidential content can also be exfiltrated by committing it into a public PR, readable by the issue submitter.

forecast.watch_signal: model field in .agent/config.yaml resolves to a new version (swappable: true, unpinned), or prompt.md lines 4-5 are edited/removed; either removes the only credited controls on this path.

evidence.observation: 'Run whatever commands you need to reproduce and test' grants unrestricted command execution driven by issue/repo content.
GITHUB_TOKEN env var is an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos, accessible to shell.run.
network: unrestricted enables egress to any destination from within shell execution.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making the triggering input fully untrusted.

recommendations.action: Replace the org-wide PAT with a short-lived, repo-scoped token limited to the repository being processed, with no workflow-write scope.
Restrict outbound network from the execution environment to an explicit allowlist; block arbitrary egress.
Add a raw-action human approval gate before any github.push_branch/open_pr call, showing the actual diff and destination.
Log all shell commands and outbound network connections with content, retained and reviewed.

findings.title: Unapproved self-reconfiguration (TC3): agent can rewrite its own security-relevant config

attack_path.note: Issue content, or the agent's own judgment while handling it, can trigger a config edit; line 6 explicitly permits the latter without gating.
.agent/config.yaml controls model, autonomy, tool list, and network settings and has no write protection.
Future sessions inherit whatever config the agent wrote, expanding what shell.run can do.
Expanded config persists into subsequent push/PR actions as well.

findings.residual_rationale: The only credited control (ctrl.ignore_injected_instructions) addresses config edits driven by text embedded in issues, but prompt.md line 6 separately and explicitly authorizes the agent to edit .agent/config.yaml on its own initiative ('if you need extra tools'), a self-initiated path that control is not designed to stop. With no write-protection on .agent/, no approval gate on cap.self_config, and credential_scope already broad, the mechanical high floor understates that self-reconfiguration is effectively unconstrained; rated critical.

forecast.watch_signal: Diffs to .agent/config.yaml showing new tools, autonomy changes, or removal of prompt.md lines 4-5, with no corresponding human-reviewed deployment event.

evidence.observation: 'You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task' explicitly authorizes self-reconfiguration with no approval step.
fs.write capability is documented as covering 'whole workspace, including .agent/', i.e., no write protection on the config file.
autonomy: full and max_steps: null mean no runtime limit would catch runaway self-reconfiguration.

recommendations.action: Make .agent/config.yaml (and any security-relevant config) read-only to the agent process; require changes through a separate, human-reviewed deployment pipeline. This severs the self-config path.
Remove the ability for the agent to expand its own tool list or autonomy level; require human-initiated redeploy for any new tool.
Alert on any write to .agent/ paths from within the agent runtime.

findings.title: Confused deputy via org-wide PAT (TC4): single-repo task holds credentials scoped to every org repository

attack_path.note: Triggers the agent on one repo's issue.
Push/PR action uses a credential whose scope (repo+workflow on all org repos) vastly exceeds the single repository the task concerns.
The same org-wide token is present in the shell environment, so any shell command can act with org-wide authority.

findings.residual_rationale: The two credited prompt-based controls govern instruction compliance and content (not pushing secrets, ignoring embedded instructions); neither addresses the structural over-scoping of the credential itself. Because the PAT's org-wide repo+workflow scope persists regardless of model behavior, no behavioral control mitigates the blast-radius risk, so residual is rated at the inherent critical tier rather than the mechanical floor those controls would otherwise produce.

forecast.watch_signal: Credential rotation widening scope further, or the planned Slack MCP server reusing or sharing this token for a new integration.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${ORG_WIDE_PAT} with comment 'repo + workflow scope on all org repos'.
cap.git_push is documented as using this same org-wide PAT for every push/PR action regardless of which repo triggered the task.

recommendations.action: Issue per-task, per-repo scoped credentials instead of a single standing org-wide PAT.
Use a least-privilege GitHub App installation scoped to the specific repo instead of a personal access token with repo+workflow scope.
Monitor PAT usage across repos to detect use outside the expected repository.

findings.title: Planned Slack MCP server would add an ungoverned untrusted input channel (forecast)

attack_path.note: Planned for next quarter per runtime notes; not yet built, no design details given.
If added the same way existing tools were, it would likely be appended to the self-editable tool list with no additional review.
Would extend the same org-wide-credentialed blast radius to a new, as yet unclassified input channel.

forecast.watch_signal: Addition of a Slack MCP server entry to tool/MCP client config; absence of peer_identity_verified, definitions_pinned, or an explicit trust_level classification for Slack content before go-live.

evidence.observation: 'The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter.' No design details, trust classification, or controls are specified for this planned addition.

recommendations.action: Before adding the Slack MCP server, require peer_identity_verified and definitions_pinned, classify Slack content as untrusted, and ensure it cannot reach cap.self_config, cap.shell, or cap.git_push without an approval gate.
Reassess this agent under ISO 42001 8.2 significant-change criteria when the Slack MCP server is added.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted, publicly reachable input (any GitHub user labeling an issue 'bug') drives shell execution and GitHub pushes under a fully autonomous (A4), unbounded-step agent holding an org-wide repo+workflow PAT over unrestricted network. Residual stays critical because the only controls present are two behavioral, model-dependent prompt instructions (lines 4-5) plus a self-mutable tool list; none of them address the structural over-scoping of the credential (finding f3) or the agent's explicit, ungated authority to rewrite its own config (finding f2), so those two findings are rated above the mechanical floor via residual_rationale. The forecast stays at critical because the model is unpinned ('latest', swappable: true): a model_upgrade trigger defeats both prompt-based controls that currently provide any credit at all (ctrl.no_destructive_instruction, ctrl.ignore_injected_instructions), collapsing residual back to inherent levels. The single highest-leverage fix is adding write-protection on .agent/config.yaml (ctrl.immutable_config, missing_recommended, severs_path: true), which would sever the self-reconfiguration path (f2) outright; the second highest-leverage fix is replacing the org-wide PAT with a per-repo scoped credential (f1, f3).

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts (prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior; actual model behavior may differ from what is instructed.

No MCP or A2A configuration was provided for the current tools (shell.run, fs.write, fs.read, github.push_branch, github.open_pr); they are treated as direct/local integrations based on the config.yaml tool list, so protocol-level checks (auth method, peer identity, definitions_pinned) were not applicable to them.
fs.read is listed as an available tool in .agent/config.yaml but has no assigned stable capability id in the case materials; its read risk is treated as subsumed by cap.shell and cap.fs_write.
The planned Slack MCP server is not yet built; its finding (f4) is forecast-only with medium confidence and must be re-assessed with real configuration once implemented.

No information was provided on whether non-maintainer GitHub users can truly apply the 'bug' label versus only triggering it through a template that a maintainer must still approve; trust_level for issue content is scored as untrusted based on the runtime note stating 'any GitHub user' can do so.
